transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining, appreciate you making time. quick roll call?
[00:07] Priya Patel: Priya here, Head of Platform at Aperture.
[00:09] Liam O'Connor: Liam, CTO.
[00:11] Jorge Ramos: Jorge, SRE.
[00:13] Sofia Kim: Sofia, security.
[00:15] Ethan Ruiz: Ethan from Redwood, SE.
[00:18] Maya Chen: Awesome. Agenda — quick overview of your reliability requirements, then go into routing/fallback options and then map to Hosted/Dedicated/Private fit, plus next steps. Sound good?
[00:28] Priya Patel: Yep, sounds good.
[00:30] Liam O'Connor: Good.
[00:31] Jorge Ramos: Yep.
[00:33] Maya Chen: Cool. So can you give us the current context, Priya — what are the SLAs you need, and what does peak look like for you?
[00:40] Priya Patel: Sure. We're a payments company — so latency and availability are both critical. We aim for a 99.95% availability for our auth flows and p99 latency under 200ms for the short text prompts used in fraud scoring. Peak windows are US business hours and end-of-day settlement windows, approx 3x baseline traffic.
[01:03] Jorge Ramos: And we have regulatory constraints — certain cardholder data and logs need to live in our environment for 90 days, so we were exploring Private deployment options.
[01:13] Sofia Kim: Also SOC two, ISO stuff— we need audit logs, KMS integration, and SSO.
[01:19] Ethan Ruiz: Right, totally. We see those needs a lot. On the SLA piece: Redwood Hosted can back a 99.9% at baseline with SLA tiers for Dedicated that go to 99.95% with reserved capacity. For stricter, Private deployment with your own infra is the usual pathway.
[01:34] Liam O'Connor: When you say reserved capacity, what's the failure behavior? Like if a zone goes down — do you have automatic multi-region failover? How does session state or KV cache behave?
[01:46] Ethan Ruiz: Good question. We route via smart routing layer — requests are routed by policy: latency-first, cost-first, or region-first. For multi-region failover we maintain warm model replicas and we replicate KV cache state asynchronously; there's a short warmup if you fail to new region, but we also do prefix caching to reduce cold starts. In practice you'll see a small p99 bump during failover windows.
[02:08] Maya Chen: To add — we have canary & automatic fallback policies. If the primary model crosses error or latency thresholds we can automatically route to a cheaper, compatible model variant or fall back to a cached response depending on policy.
[02:20] Priya Patel: The fallback to cheaper model — we'd need strict quality signoffs. For fraud scoring, false negatives are a real risk. Can we keep a canary that validates for quality before serving?
[02:32] Ethan Ruiz: Yep, you can set a canary traffic slice. Redwood Optimize can monitor quality metrics tied to your prompt suites — you can pause automatic fallback until the canary passes a quality threshold. There's a human-in-loop option too.
[02:45] Jorge Ramos: How about the routing consistency — if we split traffic across regions during warmup, do we risk inconsistent decisions for the same user mid-flow?
[02:55] Ethan Ruiz: We support session affinity rules and sticky routing for a key so a user session can be pinned to a region for X minutes. Also, for critical flows you can opt to route to region-first to avoid cross-region variance.
[03:08] Liam O'Connor: OK. About caching — you mentioned KV cache replication is async. Any numbers on RPO/RTO for that cache?
[03:16] Ethan Ruiz: For async replication we typically see under 60s for KV sync under normal load. But that depends on traffic and sequence lengths; very long sequences can increase propagation. If you need tighter, Dedicated with co-located cache or Private deploy with a sync layer gives lower RPOs.
[03:31] Priya Patel: We can't accept a 60s window for some of our scoring flows — we need near real-time. So Dedicated or Private sounds more likely. But cost is a concern.
[03:41] Maya Chen: Totally understandable. Dedicated can be sized for predictable throughput and you can reserve burst capacity. There are also cost controls: intelligent batching, quantization profiles — Redwood Optimize can recommend those to hit your latency targets while reducing cost.
[03:56] Sofia Kim: For Private deployment — what's the network model? Do you host in our VPC or is it a packaged on-prem? We need HSM/KMS for key custody.
[04:05] Ethan Ruiz: Private deployment options: 1) VPC-hosted — control plane managed by Redwood but data plane sits in your VPC, keys in your KMS. 2) Full on-prem appliance — offline option with tighter control. Both support KMS/HSM integrations and audit logs.
[04:20] Priya Patel: Any differences in fallback and multi-region behavior in Private?
[04:24] Ethan Ruiz: In VPC mode you can set up cross-region VPC peering or rely on your existing multi-region network — Redwood's routing still applies, but you have more control of replication topology. On-prem can be more manual — you'd define your replication boundaries.
[04:37] Liam O'Connor: Ok, practical question — during an incident, can Redwood do automatic degrade to cached results or do we have to orchestrate that from our side?
[04:46] Maya Chen: We have built-in circuit breakers and degrade strategies — you can configure automatic fallback to cached outputs, lower-cost model variants, or route to a synthetic safe response. These can be triggered by domain-specific error budgets and both automated and manual triggers are supported.
[04:59] Jorge Ramos: Any guardrails to avoid silent quality drift when falling back? We don't want undetected low-quality outputs during a prolonged outage.
[05:07] Ethan Ruiz: That's where integrated quality monitors come in — Redwood can tie fallback events into alerts and maintain a histogram of quality scores, and we can require manual approval to continue fallback after X minutes. Also all degraded outputs are tagged in logs for auditing.
[05:20] Sofia Kim: For compliance we need full traceability of model invocations and who authorized fallbacks. Is that captured?
[05:25] Ethan Ruiz: Yes — audit logs include policy triggers, operator actions, and trace IDs. You can export these to your SIEM.
[05:31] Priya Patel: Good. What about SLA credits — how do you measure downtime at token-level services?
[05:36] Maya Chen: SLA measurement is based on request success and latency against SLO windows. For Hosted we publish historical uptime and you'll get credits if SLA isn't met per contract. Dedicated has tighter, contract-backed SLOs. Private deployments have support SLAs but uptime of your infra is customer-managed.
[05:53] Liam O'Connor: Would you be able to simulate a zone outage and show what client latency looks like in a POC?
[05:58] Ethan Ruiz: Absolutely — we can run a chaos sim in the POC: fail a region and capture p50/p95/p99 and error rates. We'll template a runbook and share.
[06:07] Priya Patel: That would be great. Also want to validate fail-open vs fail-closed behavior — in payments we probably want fail-closed for auth, but for passive scoring maybe fail-open with fallback.
[06:18] Jorge Ramos: Yes — flow-level policy. How granular are policies?
[06:21] Ethan Ruiz: Policies are per-route and per-model. You can tag routes (auth, scoring, enrichment) and set different fallback rules and thresholds for each.
[06:30] Maya Chen: Quick real-world note: some customers run hybrid — Hosted for non-critical low-cost flows, Dedicated for auth flows, and Private for highest-compliance workloads. That lets you balance cost and risk.
[06:43] Liam O'Connor: Sounds reasonable. On the procurement side — is Private a long lead? How long to stand up a VPC private deployment?
[06:51] Ethan Ruiz: VPC Private can typically be stood up in 4–8 weeks depending on networking and approvals; on-prem appliances are longer — often 8–12 weeks. Dedicated reservations can be provisioned in 2–3 weeks if capacity is available.
[07:03] Priya Patel: For our timeline — we plan a pilot in May and a wider roll in Q3. So we need something quick to validate resilience and the quality thresholds. Hosted pilot with chaos sim sounds like a way to validate routing/fallback without waiting for Private.
[07:18] Maya Chen: Agreed. Let's capture the pilot scope then — Ethan, what would you need to run the sim?
[07:23] Ethan Ruiz: We'll need: sample traffic replay or a traffic profile, a few representative prompt sets for quality checks, defined routes (auth vs scoring), and a test key. Also permission to run a simulated region failover. Priya, can you provide traffic profiles?
[07:39] Priya Patel: Yes, we'll share our 48hr traffic dump and a smaller replay set and mark sensitive fields.
[07:45] Jorge Ramos: We'll scrub PII and tokens before sending.
[07:48] Sofia Kim: Security will need to review the security pack before we hand over more.
[07:52] Maya Chen: Totally. I'll send the SOC2 and network design to Sofia.
[07:56] Ethan Ruiz: I'll prepare a checklist and a benchmarking spreadsheet — it'll include the chaos sim scenario, the metrics we'll collect (p50/p95/p99, error rate, cache RPO), and suggested canary thresholds.
[08:07] Liam O'Connor: About pricing — can you ballpark Dedicated for our QPS?
[08:12] Maya Chen: We can give ranges — I'll include a Dedicated tier cost estimate and Hosted usage projection based on your 3x peak. We'll flag the unit economics tradeoffs for using caching and batching.
[08:23] Priya Patel: One more on audit: If fallback happened, we need a forensics snapshot — logs and the input that triggered the fallback. Is the raw input retained?
[08:33] Ethan Ruiz: Raw inputs retention depends on deployment: Hosted redwood stores request logs per tenant with configurable retention; Dedicated supports you controlling retention, and Private you manage logs. We can set retention to match your policy and support redaction hooks.
[08:46] Jorge Ramos: Perfect.
[08:48] Maya Chen: Running low on time. Quick recap: 1) Aperture will send traffic profile and prompt sets. 2) Redwood will send security pack and benchmarking template. 3) Redwood to run initial model perf run and prepare chaos sim plan. 4) Schedule POC sync week of 2026-04-13. Anything missing?
[09:07] Priya Patel: That covers it.
[09:09] Liam O'Connor: No, sounds good.
[09:10] Sofia Kim: We'll review security pack when you send it.
[09:12] Maya Chen: Awesome. Thanks all — we'll follow up with artifacts and a calendar invite.
[09:16] (call ends)
